---
title: "Transforming a response"
---

The [straight-line mean](simple-linear-regression.qmd) does not determine the scale on which the response should be modeled. Reaction times are positive and often right skewed. Most responses cluster in a relatively narrow fast range, while a smaller number extend far into the slow tail. An ordinary linear regression fitted to raw milliseconds can consequently predict negative values and leave strongly skewed residuals.

One possible response is to transform the measurement before fitting the model. For a positive response $Y_i$, define

$$
Z_i=\log Y_i.
$$

The regression is then a model for the conditional mean of log response time:

$$
Z_i
=
\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i,
\qquad
\epsilon_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2).
$$

The logarithm is the new concept. The linear regression machinery is unchanged.

The transformation changes the scale on which the model treats effects as additive. On the raw scale, a linear model treats
equal millisecond differences as comparable. On the log scale, it treats equal
ratios as comparable.

## Examining what the logarithm does

Compare three response times:

| milliseconds | natural log |
|---:|---:|
| 400 | 5.99 |
| 800 | 6.68 |
| 1600 | 7.38 |

Doubling from 400 to 800 milliseconds adds about $.69$ on the log scale. Doubling again from 800 to 1600 adds the same amount. Equal ratios on the original scale become equal differences on the log scale.

This property makes a linear coefficient multiplicative after back-transformation.

The reverse is also true. Equal differences on the log scale become equal
ratios on the original scale. Since

$$
\log(2y)-\log(y)=\log 2,
$$

doubling any positive response produces the same log difference. But adding 400
milliseconds does not. The change from 400 to 800 is a doubling, while the
change from 800 to 1200 is only a factor of 1.5.

## Interpreting a coefficient as a ratio

Suppose $x_i$ marks a high-surprisal word and

$$
\beta_1=.08.
$$

The expected log response differs by $.08$. Exponentiating gives

$$
e^{.08}\approx1.083.
$$

Thus the fitted geometric mean response is about 8.3 percent larger in the
high-surprisal condition, under the model.

For a small coefficient, $100\beta_1$ is a rough percentage approximation. Reporting $100(e^{\beta_1}-1)$ gives the exact multiplicative interpretation.

If $\beta_1=-.10$, then

$$
e^{-.10}\approx.905.
$$

The fitted geometric mean is multiplied by about $.905$, a decrease of about
9.5 percent. The approximation $100\beta_1=-10$ percent is close but not exact.

For a two-unit predictor contrast, the ratio is

$$
e^{2\beta_1}.
$$

Coefficients remain expressed per predictor unit even after the response has
been transformed.

## Checking the transformation in R

```{r}
#| label: inspect-log-response-transformation
#| echo: true
response_time <- c(400, 800, 1600)

data.frame(
  response_time = response_time,
  log_response_time = log(response_time),
  recovered_response_time = exp(log(response_time))
)
```

Exponentiating recovers the original positive measurements up to numerical
precision. The transformation is one-to-one on positive values, so no ordering
information is lost. Its spacing changes.

The positivity restriction matters. A response of zero has log value
$-\infty$, and a negative response has no real-valued logarithm. A log response
model thus requires a measurement whose meaningful support is strictly
positive.

## Back-transformation of a mean

If

$$
\log Y\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),
$$

then

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y]=e^{\mu+\sigma^2/2},
$$

not merely $e^\mu$. The quantity $e^\mu$ is the median of the implied lognormal distribution.

Why does the mean differ? Exponentiation is nonlinear. Large positive log-scale
deviations increase raw responses more than equally large negative deviations
decrease them. The right tail thus pulls the raw-scale mean above $e^\mu$.

Suppose

$$
\mu=6
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sigma=.30.
$$

Then the raw-scale median is

$$
e^6\approx403.4,
$$

while the raw-scale mean is

$$
e^{6+.30^2/2}
=e^{6.045}
\approx421.9.
$$

The difference grows with $\sigma$. A single exponentiated fitted mean does not
capture it.

This distinction matters when predictions are returned to milliseconds. A model for mean log time is not automatically a model for mean raw time.

The quantity $e^{\widehat\mu}$ cannot automatically be interpreted as a raw-scale mean. That interpretation silently replaces a median-like
quantity with a mean. The correction depends on the modeled residual
distribution and its variance.

## Treating the transformation as part of the model

A transformation changes the response scale, residual pattern, coefficient interpretation, and predictive target. It should not be selected only because a histogram looks more symmetric.

The model should be checked on both scales. A satisfactory log-scale residual plot can coexist with poor predictions of the slow raw-time tail. Conversely, a raw-scale family such as a lognormal or shifted distribution may represent the measurement process more directly.

This is not a contest in which the most symmetric histogram wins. The scale of additivity should
match the theoretical comparison and the response-generating process. If a
processing account predicts proportional slowing, a log scale may state that
claim directly. If it predicts an additive millisecond cost, a log response
changes the target.

## Reporting the modeled quantity

A complete coefficient interpretation states both scales. For instance: "A
one-bit surprisal increase was associated with a $.08$ increase in expected log
reading time, corresponding to an 8.3 percent multiplicative change in the
fitted geometric mean." This statement does not call the exponentiated value a
raw-scale mean.

Predicted raw observations can instead be generated from the complete log-scale
response model and summarized on the raw scale. That procedure retains residual
variation rather than exponentiating only the conditional mean.
